name: Melchezidek Searles
headline: I build market systems with a researcher's discipline.
intro: Economics student, self-taught engineer, and founder of SkyQuant. I turn noisy market data into reproducible systems — then keep testing until the evidence is boring.
shortBio: I am an economics student at CUNY and a self-taught software engineer based in New York. I build research and execution systems for markets, with a bias toward reproducibility, clean data, and evidence that survives an audit.

projects.name: SkyQ RANGE
projects.summary: A causal one-minute ETF research engine that treats costs, ambiguous fills, and negative results as part of the product.
projects.description: A Python and PostgreSQL research core with a React control center. The published record covers 67,271 SPY trades and 32,356 QQQ trades over 23 years, with stop-first fills and modeled costs. The same geometry was then tested on ten futures contracts and rejected after costs — a falsification record, not a hidden failure.

caseStudy.problem: A one-minute result is only useful if the costs and fills that decide it are visible.
caseStudy.built: A causal Python and PostgreSQL engine that makes stop-first fills, modeled costs, and cross-asset checks part of the test.
caseStudy.evidence: 67,271 SPY trades, 32,356 QQQ trades, 16/24 positive SPY years, and ten futures contracts publicly rejected after costs.

projects.name: SkyQ Sigma S
projects.summary: An execution-aware backtest and paper-trading system built across five broker and market-data APIs.
projects.description: A 43,249-trade replay engine with a 160-test suite, crash recovery, order reconciliation, an NYSE-aware calendar, and a tick-to-bar path verified against broker data. The engine, methodology, and walkthrough are available; the live rule set stays private.

caseStudy.problem: A backtest is not production evidence when restarts and broker reconciliation are untested.
caseStudy.built: An execution-aware paper engine with crash recovery, order reconciliation, and an NYSE-aware calendar across five data APIs.
caseStudy.evidence: 43,249 replayed trades and a 160-test suite; the methodology is available while the live rule set stays private.

projects.name: SkyQuant Capital
projects.summary: A first fund built in the right order: company-funded pilot, public evidence, then an anchor-led vehicle.
projects.description: A 12-month real-money pilot using $2,000–$5,000 of saved company capital and one SPY share. The proposed next step is a $25M–$50M fund with a 1/10 founders class, 1.5/15 standard terms, a 5% hurdle, and a high-water mark. No fund exists today.

caseStudy.problem: A first fund should not be sold before there is a record.
caseStudy.built: A company-funded pilot with saved capital, one SPY share, monthly reconciliation, and a written operating standard.
caseStudy.evidence: $2k–$5k pilot capital, a 12-month public record target, and a proposed $25M–$50M fund only after evidence. No fund today.

principles.title: Measure the boring thing.
principles.body: Costs, fills, calendars, time zones, and the difference between two data feeds decide whether a result is real.

principles.title: Keep the negative result.
principles.body: A test that rejects a strategy is still evidence. I publish the cross-asset failures next to the wins.

principles.title: Make it reproducible.
principles.body: Checksums, tests, fixed data windows, and written assumptions are part of the work — not cleanup after it.

principles.title: Explain it plainly.
principles.body: Teaching code to beginners is the same discipline as defending a model: if the idea is clear, the language can be simple.

resumeSummary: Self-taught software engineer and economics student in New York. I build reproducible market-research and execution systems in Python, SQL, and TypeScript, with a strong bias toward testing, data integrity, and clear written evidence. Teacher by practice; future economics professor by plan.
careerGoal: Near term, I want to work on Python backend, data, or market-systems teams where correctness matters and the domain is complex. Long term, I want to teach economics and keep building research software that makes markets easier to understand.
